description: We’re second-year CS & IT students tackling the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer for the first time. We’re beginners, but curious, fast learners who enjoy web dev and making science fun for kids. Join a friendly team where every idea counts and we aim for a polished, demo-ready game. Looking for: UI/UX or illustration, game dev/3D (Unity, Three.js), frontend (JS/React), educational content writing, and video/pitch editing. Space fans and beginners welcome!
summary:
Outpost Zero is a zero-install, browser-based 3D lunar and Martian outpost simulator built for students ages 7–12. Traditional space education often relies on static facts that show mission outcomes without teaching the engineering logic behind them, or complex math that loses young learners' attention.

Our simulator addresses this challenge by turning deep-space survival into tactile gameplay where no choice is free. Players command an outpost at the Moon’s Shackleton Crater or Mars’ Jezero Crater, wiring 3D power grids, mining regolith, and balancing competing subsystems across Power, Oxygen, Water, Food, and Radiation Shielding. Every decision carries a real compounding cost: switching greenhouses to high-calorie CSA Arctic potatoes prevents starvation but drains 40% more water from oxygen generators, while Mars light-time radio delays force crews to solve emergencies before Earth can respond.

Grounded in live NASA DONKI solar weather, RadLab radiation dosimetry, OSDR space biology, and CSA agricultural science, Outpost Zero transforms real NASA telemetry into unforgettable STEM decisions.
details:
Outpost Zero is a browser-based, zero-install 3D engineering and resource-management simulator designed for students ages 7–12. Players take command of a four-astronaut surface habitat at one of two real exploration sites: the Moon’s Shackleton Crater Rim (89.9∘S89.9^\circ\text{S}89.9∘S) or Mars’ Jezero Crater Delta (18.38∘N18.38^\circ\text{N}18.38∘N).

Instead of allowing infinite sandbox expansion, the simulation enforces strict zero-sum engineering trade-offs where no choice is free:

  • Tactile 3D Base & Microgrid Management: Players mine surface regolith and water-ice with a 3D mining laser, construct modular structures (Solar Arrays, Nuclear Reactors, Oxygen Generators, Water Recyclers, Geodesic Greenhouses, Regolith Shield Mounds, and Decontamination Scrubbers), and physically link glowing 3D power conduits from the central dome to each module.
  • Power vs. Life Support Budgeting: During lunar nights or Martian dust storms, solar efficiency drops sharply. Throttling Life Support to Eco Mode (70%) preserves overnight battery reserves, but reduces oxygen production and water recovery by 22%—teaching compounding resource debt.
  • CSA Space & Arctic Hydroponics Trade-Offs: Grounded in the Canadian Space Agency’s (CSA) Food Production on the Moon and in Remote Areas toolkit, players switch greenhouse crops in real time between Mizuna Lettuce (low water/power draw, modest calories), Tomatosphere Tomatoes (balanced yield + morale boost), and CSA Arctic Dwarf Potatoes (+100% caloric output to prevent starvation, but drains +40% more water and +25% more power from oxygen systems).
  • Live Space Weather & Radiation Dosimetry: Connected live to NASA’s DONKI API, real M-class and X-class solar flares trigger surface radiation alarms. Grounded in NASA RadLab baselines (LRO CRaTER at 1.37 mSv/day on the Moon; Curiosity RAD at 0.64 mSv/sol on Mars), players must route their crew inside the shielded habitat airlock or spend scarce water and power running decontamination scrubbers.
  • Deep Space Network (DSN) Light-Time Communication Delay: Requesting an emergency engineering supply uplink models real radio propagation speed (300,000 km/s300,000\text{ km/s}300,000 km/s)—taking 1.3 seconds on the Moon versus a prolonged DSN Transmission Countdown on Mars (representing the 4-to-24-minute real one-way light delay), proving why deep-space crews cannot rely on instant rescue from Earth.
  • In-Game NASA OSDR Search Engine: Players and teachers can query NASA’s Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) Search API directly inside the game using kid-friendly topic pills (plant, bone, muscle, radiation, sleep, immune) to inspect the real spaceflight experiments behind their survival dilemmas.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Closing the STEM Translation Gap: Bridges the gap between passive space posters (too simple to teach trade-offs) and professional mission-planning spreadsheets (too dense for elementary and middle schoolers).
  • Zero Barrier to Entry for Classrooms: Requires zero downloads, zero user accounts, and zero specialized hardware. Any student, teacher, or judge can launch the full 3D simulation instantaneously via a single web link on desktop laptops, Chromebooks, tablets, or mobile phones.
  • Built-In Assessment & Replayability: Includes a 1-click Judge & Classroom Tour that walks users through all core NASA/CSA scientific constraints in 60 seconds, while procedural resource nodes and live space-weather telemetry make every playthrough unique.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Stack

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+).
  • 3D Graphics & Rendering: Three.js (WebGL r128) featuring custom fractional Brownian motion (fbm) procedural crater terrain, dynamic 24-hour solar elevation lighting, animated quadratic Bezier power cables, and shared PBR material pooling (SHARED_MAT) for 60 FPS performance on low-end school devices.
    1. NASA Open APIs (api.nasa.gov): Live DONKI Solar Flare (FLR), Coronal Mass Ejection (CME), and Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD) endpoints with curated offline fallbacks.
    2. NASA Open Science Data Repository (osdr.nasa.gov/osdr/data/search): Live keyword search API for space biology datasets.
    3. NASA RadLab Dosimetry (visualization.osdr.nasa.gov/radlab): Authentic absorbed dose rates from ISS TEPC/DosTel, Lunar LRO CRaTER, and Martian MSL RAD.
    4. NASA Mars Trek & Artemis III Geodesy: Real coordinate, elevation, and illumination profiles.
    5. CSA Space Food Toolkit: Crop transpiration, LED lighting demand, and caloric yield models.

How Our Project Is Creative & Factors Considered

  • Audience & Cognitive Load (Ages 7–12): We deliberately avoided overwhelming young players with 10+ spreadsheet currencies. Instead, we distilled deep-space survival into five intuitive top-bar pills (⚡ Power, 💨 Air, 💧 Water, 🌱 Food, 🛡️ Rays) paired with plain-language tooltips that explain terms like Sol, Regolith, and Millisievert (mSv) in context.
  • Honest Data Attribution: Every trade-off popup and subsystem card explicitly cites the exact NASA or CSA dataset driving the math, and clearly distinguishes between live API telemetry and curated historical fallback data so students and educators know they are engaging with authentic space science.
